You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:

- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld

Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The first thing my father did when he retired was move the kitchen clock eleven inches to the left.

“It was fine where it was,” my mother said.

“It was behind the door.”

“Only when the door was open.”

He considered this a decisive point in his favor. She considered it a description of how doors work.

When I came home that weekend, the clock was off the wall altogether. It lay faceup on the table, ticking beneath a dish towel. My parents were out buying peaches. In the clock’s old spot was a pale circle where twenty-three years of cooking had failed to reach the paint. In the new spot was a small, unexpectedly violent hole.

I lifted the towel. Taped to the back of the clock was a photograph.

My mother, maybe thirty, stood barefoot on an unfamiliar lawn. She wore red shorts. There was a baby on her hip and a hose in her hand, and she was watering a little boy who stood quite solemnly in a galvanized tub. On the back, in my father’s block capitals, someone had written: JULY. THE POOL.

I was the little boy. The baby was my sister. The lawn was unfamiliar because it had become a driveway before I was old enough to remember it.

When my parents returned, I showed them the photograph.

“Oh,” my mother said. “My good shorts.”

My father put the peaches in a colander. “I wondered where that went.”

“Why was it on the clock?”

“It kept slipping.”

“The clock?”

“The photograph. It was tucked into the frame of the mirror in the hall. Every time anybody shut the front door, down it went. I got tired of picking it up.”

“So you taped it somewhere nobody would ever see it?”

He turned on the faucet. “Well, you saw it.”

We ate the peaches standing at the sink. They were ripe enough that sitting down with one would have required planning. My mother studied the photograph again. She couldn’t remember who had taken it. My father suggested Uncle Ray, but Uncle Ray had worked Saturdays.

“How do you know it was a Saturday?” I asked.

“Because that was the day we washed the dog.”

There was no dog in the photograph.

“He’d gotten out of the tub,” she explained. “That’s why you were allowed in it.”

For years, when I thought of my childhood, I thought of the things my parents had arranged for me: swimming lessons, birthday parties, the miserable educational stop at a salt mine on the way to the coast. I had never given much thought to being permitted, on a hot morning, to stand in the water a dog had finished with.

“Did I like it?”

“You wanted a turn with the hose,” my mother said. “You always liked the job better.”

She handed me the photograph. I put it in my wallet, where, over the next several months, it acquired a white crease through the lawn.

We hung the clock in its original spot. My father patched the other hole. He used a paint sample from the basement labeled KITCHEN, which turned out to mean the kitchen as it had looked two kitchens ago. The result was a neat green square on a yellow wall.

“There,” he said, with the peculiar satisfaction of a man who has made a problem smaller and more definite.

My mother looked at the square. Then she opened the kitchen door all the way.

From where we stood, you couldn’t see it.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A compact literary family vignette built around a household clock, an old photograph, and the shifting meanings of childhood memory.

## Grounded reading
The voice is dryly observant and affectionate without becoming sentimental. Its pathos comes through small discrepancies: the parents’ different recollections, the vanished lawn, and a photo kept out of sight because it kept slipping. The narrator’s discovery reframes childhood not as a set of planned activities but as a moment of ordinary permission and play. The ending invites the reader to notice how family history survives in practical gestures and domestic repairs, even when nobody can quite agree on what happened.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample centers on aging parents, everyday disagreements, and memory lodged in objects: the clock, the photograph, the peaches, and the mismatched paint patch. It treats care as something quiet and imperfect—preserving a picture, making room for a child with the hose—rather than as an explicit declaration. The mood balances gentle comedy with a modest ache for a landscape and childhood that have disappeared.

## Evidence line
> There was no dog in the photograph.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent, distinctive attention to domestic objects and understated family tenderness makes this sample meaningful evidence of a particular expressive sensibility.
